analysis.one_liner: Makes it much harder for investors to win securities fraud lawsuits against companies, executives, and their advisors.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: introduced in August 1992 with 20 cosponsors, it sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee and died when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules investors use to sue for securities fraud. It would replace shared 'joint and several' liability so each defendant pays only its assigned share, raise the bar for proving fraud to 'clear and convincing' evidence, count only knowing deception — not reckless conduct — as fraud, impose a strict one-year deadline after discovery (and five years overall) to sue, and shift attorney fees to losing plaintiffs. It would also restrict who can represent shareholder class actions and cap what class representatives collect.
analysis.who_benefits: Publicly traded companies, their officers and directors, and the professionals who serve them — accountants, investment bankers, and lawyers who face suit as aiders and abettors. They would face fewer, harder-to-win, shorter-lived fraud suits and would no longer be jointly on the hook for the full damage award when other defendants cannot pay. Defendants who prevail would also be able to collect their fees from losing plaintiffs, which would discourage many small investors from suing at all.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public companies, executives, auditors, and investment banks

how_it_helps.text: A defendant would be liable for the full judgment only if found to have committed 'knowing securities fraud' — actual knowledge of a false statement and that others would rely on it; reckless conduct would not qualify [S3].

Otherwise each defendant would pay only its percentage of responsibility, with no right to collect the unpaid share from other defendants — removing the incentive for small defendants to settle to escape 'deep pockets' exposure [S3].

Plaintiffs would have to prove scienter (a guilty state of mind) by clear and convincing evidence and plead facts suggesting it, a far higher bar than the ordinary standards used in federal court [S3].
Suits would have to be filed within one year of discovery (or when reasonable diligence should have revealed it) and no more than five years after the violation, cutting off older claims [S3].
The losing party would generally pay the winner's attorney fees and expenses unless its position was 'substantially justified,' and even discovery disputes would carry automatic fee-shifting [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Investors who lost money to securities fraud. Under the bill they would face a higher burden of proof, a much shorter filing window, the risk of paying the defendant's fees if they lost, and recoveries reduced by what the SEC already clawed back — while companies, executives, accountants, and bankers would escape joint liability and recklessness-based claims. The bill's stated purpose was to curb allegedly 'meritless' suits it said were driving up capital costs and pushing companies toward bankruptcy [S3].

drawbacks.text: Raising the proof standard to 'clear and convincing' and excluding reckless conduct would bar many fraud claims that are real but hard to prove at that level — securities fraud is typically proven through patterns of conduct, not smoking-gun admissions.

The one-year discovery deadline and fee-shifting against losing plaintiffs would deter small investors from bringing legitimate claims at all, since losing could mean owing the corporation's legal bills [S3].

The strongest good-faith objection in its favor: runaway strike suits do exist, and joint and several liability can force a minor participant to pay the entire judgment when the main wrongdoer is insolvent — a genuine unfairness the bill's proportionate-liability scheme addresses [S3].

Its anti-abuse provisions for class actions — limiting representative plaintiffs' awards and barring lawyers who paid third parties to land the case — target real practices but were bundled with provisions that reach far beyond abusive lawsuits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real problem — some securities suits are filed mainly to extract settlements — but its remedy is far broader than the abuse. The combination of a near-impossible proof standard, elimination of reckless-misconduct liability, a one-year filing window, and fee penalties for losing plaintiffs would have shut out many meritorious claims by ordinary investors, while the benefit to companies of lower litigation risk comes with less market discipline on misleading disclosures. On balance, the costs to defrauded investors outweigh the protections for defendants.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to a subcommittee a month later, and nothing ever happened to it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Billy Tauzin (D-LA) introduced the Securities Private Enforcement Reform Act on August 11, 1992, late in the 102nd Congress [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which had jurisdiction over securities matters [S5].
On September 14, 1992 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance — where it stayed, with no hearings, markup, or floor action recorded [S5].
The bill carried 20 cosponsors, 13 Republicans and 7 Democrats, but the 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993 without the bill ever leaving committee [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, investors kept the existing rules for suing over securities fraud — including joint and several liability and recklessness-based claims — and the securities class-action plaintiffs' bar kept its business model intact. Public companies, executives, and their accountants and bankers did not get the litigation protections they sought, though nothing stopped similar proposals from returning (a narrower version of this agenda became the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act in 1995).

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defrauded investors and plaintiff-side securities lawyers

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce / Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittee and never reported it back — no markup, no hearing, no floor vote before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no voting pattern exists; its sponsorship was mixed — a Democratic sponsor with 7 Democratic and 13 Republican cosponsors.

industries.industry: Publicly traded companies and their officers and directors
industries.note: The bill would sharply cut their exposure to shareholder fraud suits — proportionate liability, a higher proof standard, and a one-year filing window. The cost falls on investors who relied on misleading disclosures.
As frequent co-defendants in fraud cases, they would gain from the new 'knowing fraud' standard, the narrow aiding-and-abetting rule, and the end of joint liability for others' share of damages.

Fee-shifting against losing plaintiffs, bans on lawyer ownership of the stock at issue and on paid case referrals, and limits on representative plaintiffs' awards would shrink their practice. Their ability to sue is the mechanism through which defrauded investors recover.

The bill targets paid professional plaintiffs and third-party solicitation of class representation — practices its findings called predatory, though these arrangements involve a small set of repeat actors.
